title: Béton mobile du Québec Inc. (Dec 2019 TCC) SR&ED Case
subject: Concrete Formulation: Six Projects Qualify, Eight Fail as Routine Trial and Error
summary: Béton mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 278, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision affecting Canadian manufacturers claiming investment tax credits. Of 14 concrete-formulation projects, six qualified and eight failed, showing that adapting known materials through trial-and-error is routine engineering, while hypothesis-driven investigation of genuine technological uncertainty can succeed despite weak contemporaneous records.
metaDescription: Read the December 2019 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling for Béton mobile du Québec Inc. and its relevance to Canadian R&D claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural History and Factual Context of the Taxpayer's Claim

On December 11, 2019, the Honourable Justice Dominique Lafleur of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) issued a landmark decision in Béton mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 278 (Dockets 2015-3425(IT)G and 2016-4491(IT)G), addressing the statutory boundaries between eligible Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) and routine industrial engineering in the manufacturing and materials sector. The appellant, Béton Mobile du Québec inc. (BMQ), is a Quebec-based concrete producer specializing in the formulation, manufacture, and on-site delivery of specialized concretes and mortars utilizing volumetric mobile concrete mixers. Unlike conventional ready-mix concrete plants that batch and mix materials in a central facility before transporting the hydrating mixture in revolving drum trucks, BMQ's mobile concrete mixers transport unmixed raw constituents—cementitious binders, aggregates, water, latex, and chemical admixtures—in separate compartments and blend them continuously on-site via an auger mixer immediately prior to pouring.

BMQ appealed reassessments issued by the Minister of National Revenue across three consecutive taxation years ending January 31, 2010, January 31, 2011, and January 31, 2012. The appeals initially concerned twenty projects for the 2010 taxation year and seven projects for each of the 2011 and 2012 taxation years, but BMQ withdrew its appeal for all but 14 distinct research and development projects (seven for 2010, three for 2011 and four for 2012), for which it claimed SR&ED expenditure deductions under section 37 and Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) in respect of salaries, materials, and subcontractor fees. BMQ contended that its projects could not rely on off-the-shelf concrete formulations or published academic literature because existing industry knowledge failed to account for the intersection of two operational constraints: the winter durability requirements of the Quebec climate, and the fact that its mixes are prepared in a mobile concrete mixer, which mixes the inputs for less time and with less force than a conventional concrete mixer. To substantiate its claims at trial—following an administrative and judicial dispute spanning approximately nine years—BMQ relied on its Form T661 filings, documentary testing records, and the viva voce testimony of two veteran professional engineers: Mr. Jacques Bertrand, co-founder and President of BMQ during the relevant periods, and Mr. Gérard Dubé, an engineer employed by BMQ.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) disallowed the SR&ED claims across all 14 projects, prompting the appeals heard on common evidence in Montreal. At trial, the Crown relied on the reviews and testimony of two CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs), both holding doctorates in mechanical engineering: Dr. Cédric Durban, a former private-sector SR&ED consultant who joined the CRA in 2009 and audited the 2010 taxation year projects, and Dr. Karim Mimoune, who joined the CRA in 2002 and audited the 2011 and 2012 taxation year projects.

The Minister's challenge rested on the position that BMQ's work across the disputed projects constituted "standard practice" or "routine engineering" rather than systematic scientific research or experimental development. Specifically, the CRA asserted that BMQ merely adapted known commercial products—such as ternary cements (Ter-C3), pozzolanic additions, latex modifiers, and new-generation superplasticizers—using established mix-design procedures and trial-and-error adjustments that were readily discernible to competent concrete professionals. Furthermore, the Crown challenged the reliability of BMQ's time sheets, arguing that hours had been estimated or rounded rather than actually recorded, and contended that several initiatives amounted to excluded activities such as characterization tests to meet industry standards, validation of existing products against applicable standards, commercial work using pre-approved mixes, or a continuation of contract-based repair work.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework in Canada

The adjudication of SR&ED claims in Canada is governed by the strict statutory definition set forth in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act"), which operates in tandem with section 37, governing the deduction of current SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada, and subsections 127(5) and 127(9), governing the calculation and earning of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits. Under subsection 248(1) of the Act, SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that is undertaken in one of three core categories: under paragraph (a), basic research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; under paragraph (b), applied research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; or under paragraph (c), experimental development, namely work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Under paragraph (d) of the definition in subsection 248(1), ancillary work—such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—qualifies only to the extent that the work is "commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of" work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c). Crucially, the statutory definition explicitly excludes several commercial and industrial activities from qualifying as SR&ED, most notably market research or sales promotion under paragraph (e), quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes under paragraph (f), research in the social sciences or the humanities under paragraph (g), prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas under paragraph (h), commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process under paragraph (i), style changes under paragraph (j), and routine data collection under paragraph (k).

To interpret and apply subsection 248(1) of the Act, Justice Lafleur anchored the court's analysis in the foundational Canadian jurisprudential framework established by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (T.C.C.), which was based on CRA Information Circular IC 86-4R3 and was confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada and reiterated in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393. Under the Northwest Hydraulic framework, the court evaluates project eligibility through five cumulative criteria, commonly referred to as the "Five Questions". First, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the court determines whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the court assesses whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Fifth, the court considers whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed.

In applying this framework, Justice Lafleur applied the two-step analytical test set out in Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597: the court must first determine whether the activities meet the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1), as interpreted through the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, with BMQ bearing the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. If a project does not meet that definition, the review ends at that step, although Justice Lafleur nonetheless indicated, for each failing project, which expenditures would have been deductible had the activities qualified. Only if a project is found to be eligible SR&ED does the court proceed to the second stage of determining whether the specific claimed expenditures—such as salaries, subcontractor fees or materials consumed or transformed—are deductible under section 37 and qualify for ITCs, having regard to the facts specific to each project.
The Court's Final Holding

Delivering a split verdict that underscores the fact-intensive nature of SR&ED litigation in the Tax Court of Canada, Justice Lafleur allowed BMQ's appeals for the 2010, 2011, and 2012 taxation years and referred the reassessments back to the Minister for reconsideration and reassessment on the basis that the activities in six projects were SR&ED and that the following amounts were deductible current expenditures and qualified for ITCs: for 2010, $3,521 for salaries, $427 for materials and $360 for subcontractor fees; for 2011, $37,668 for salaries, $2,520 for materials and $3,425 for subcontractor fees; and for 2012, $44,192 for salaries, $4,433 for materials and $9,204 for subcontractor fees—without costs. Out of the 14 disputed projects, the court ruled that six projects qualified as eligible SR&ED, while eight projects failed to meet the statutory requirements and were dismissed.

Determination of moisture in latex concrete
Ineligible (Dismissed)

Absence of technological uncertainty, since prior MTQ and U.S. studies existed and drying over time is accepted scientific knowledge; routine data collection with standard methods; no hypothesis formulated.
B-10-05
Development of a self-consolidating concrete with Ter-C3 cement
Ineligible (Dismissed)
Problem resolvable by standard procedures and routine engineering; mix placed commercially on the day of sampling; trial-and-error methodology.
B-10-07
Characterization of Ter-C3 cement
Ineligible (Dismissed)

Standard tests and adjustments routine in the industry after a change of supplier; mixes pre-approved and placed before full laboratory results; no technological advancement; reformulation by trial and error.
B-10-08
Development of a Type V concrete with Ter-C3 cement
Ineligible (Dismissed)

Large-scale trials conducted before laboratory results were known; modifications made by known methods; BMQ did not seek the cause of the increased air content; Mr. Dubé's testimony given no credibility.
B-10-09
Characterization of a new-generation plasticizer
Ineligible (Dismissed)

Effect of the admixture already known and documented; validation of standard mixes (routine testing under paragraph (f)) and data collection not in support of SR&ED; no advancement—although the court accepted that a hypothesis was formulated and the scientific method followed.
B-10-12
Development of a cavernous (no-fines) concrete with a high vacuum/void content
Ineligible (Dismissed)

No uncertainty, as the parking lot plan was approved by an engineer and the City of Laval before the work; 35% void content within the usual 30–40% range; no advancement; full-scale installation without prior testing and mainly visual observation; appeal withdrawn by BMQ during the hearing.
B-10-18
Develop a light self-compacting / self-placing mortar for a mobile concrete mixer
Eligible (Allowed)

Uncertainty as to whether a mobile mixer, which mixes for less time and with less force, could produce a mortar with 20% air content; systematic study of the causes; documentation and Mr. Dubé's testimony established the scientific method even though the product was not achieved.
B-11-01
Study of permeability to chloride ions and durability with various pozzolanic additions and cements
Ineligible (Dismissed)
Routine data collection and validation of existing mixes against a new chloride-ion permeability standard; known techniques; trial and error without analyzing why mixes failed.
B-11-04
Analysis of the influence of binders and additives on the performance of self-placing concrete
Eligible (Allowed)
System-level chemical interaction uncertainty resolved via structured hypothesis formulation and analysis.
B-11-07
Develop an ultra-fast / quick-setting mortar for installation in a marine environment
Eligible (Allowed)
Genuine technological barrier beyond standard practice; systematic investigation supported by witness testimony.
B-12-01
Development of fast / quick-setting latex-free concrete
Eligible (Allowed)
Technological uncertainty in achieving rapid setting and durability without latex polymer modification; scientific method verified.
B-12-02
Improvement of quick-setting self-compacting concrete
Ineligible (Dismissed)

Improvement of the B-11-04 product using common industry techniques (colloidal agent, analysis of weather and vibrations); trial-and-error rather than the scientific method; Mr. Dubé's testimony inconsistent with Form T661 and BMQ's 2013 letter to the CRA.
B-12-03
Development of quick-setting latex concrete screed
Eligible (Allowed)

Uncertainty because quick-setting latex concrete had never been used as a running surface on a suspension bridge, and as to surface preparation for adhesion and placement to avoid cracking; hypotheses formulated and tested.
B-12-07
Development of a repair product for roller-compacted concrete
Eligible (Allowed)

Performance of relatively new cements as roller-compacted concrete repair products unknown in current practice, with no prior large-scale tests and one mix never tested in Quebec; mixes compared under similar conditions to test hypotheses.

body.text: 2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A granular examination of Justice Lafleur's decision reveals why eight of BMQ's projects collapsed under judicial scrutiny while six succeeded on common evidentiary foundations. The disqualifications did not stem from a single isolated defect, but rather from an interconnected cascade of legal, technical, and evidentiary failures across the five criteria of the Northwest Hydraulic test and the statutory exclusions of subsection 248(1) of the Act.
Failure to Establish Scientific or Technological Uncertainty Versus Routine Engineering

The foundational threshold of any SR&ED claim in Canada is the existence of a genuine "scientific or technological uncertainty"—defined in Canadian tax law and CRA policy as whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, when the solution is not known or determinable on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience. As Justice Bowman established in Northwest Hydraulic, technological uncertainty must be a type of uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures—that is, by the techniques, procedures and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field; CRA policy additionally recognizes "system uncertainty," where individual components or materials are known, but it is impossible for a competent professional to predict how the integrated system or formulation will behave. Conversely, if a technical limitation can be resolved through standard procedures, published literature, supplier specifications, or routine engineering adjustments known to specialists in the field, no technological uncertainty exists.

In Béton mobile du Québec, BMQ failed to prove technological uncertainty on a balance of probabilities for all eight losing projects: Projects B-10-03, B-10-05, B-10-07, B-10-08, B-10-09, B-10-12, B-11-01, and B-12-02. The core analytical flaw in BMQ's position on these eight projects was conflating technical difficulty or operational unfamiliarity within the company with objective technological uncertainty in the broader scientific field. For example, in Projects B-10-05, B-10-07, and B-10-08, BMQ investigated the use of "Ter-C3" ternary cement—a blended hydraulic cement containing Portland cement and two supplementary cementitious materials—to produce self-consolidating concrete and a Type V concrete under MTQ standard 3101, a 35-megapascal ternary-cement concrete used for structural repairs. Similarly, in Project B-10-09, BMQ sought to characterize a new-generation superplasticizing admixture. Justice Lafleur noted that ternary cement was a known product whose characteristics were not new or unknown to experts, and that the effect of the new-generation superplasticizer was known and documented in the industry, so that determining the required proportions of these inputs was reasonably predictable using standard procedures and routine engineering. Although BMQ encountered practical limitations when introducing these materials into its mobile mixers, the court concluded that the solutions were readily accessible within the existing knowledge base and through current industry practices.

By contrast, in the six winning projects (Projects B-10-18, B-11-04, B-11-07, B-12-01, B-12-03, and B-12-07), BMQ successfully demonstrated genuine uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. In those projects—such as developing a lightweight self-compacting mortar with 20% air content in a mobile concrete mixer (B-10-18), formulating an ultra-fast-setting anti-washout mortar to be placed under water to seal rock at a bridge pier (B-11-07), or achieving rapid-setting, durable concrete without latex polymers (B-12-01)—the court accepted that no data existed on the mobile mixer's ability to produce such products, that the mobile mixer mixes inputs for less time and with less force than conventional mixers, that the combination of known binders and admixtures within self-compacting concrete under the mobile mixer's mixing energy had not been studied, and that documentation on the compatibility of admixtures with quick-setting (CSA) cement was almost non-existent.
Absence of Hypothesis-Driven Experimentation and Reliance on Trial-and-Error

Under the second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic, a taxpayer must formulate specific causal hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating the technological uncertainty and test those hypotheses through a "systematic investigation or search" adhering to the scientific method. In Béton mobile du Québec, Justice Lafleur cited Justice Bowman's five-stage process: first, the observation of the subject matter of the problem; second, the formulation of a clear objective; third, the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; fourth, the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and fifth, the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

A decisive factor in the disqualification of BMQ's eight unsuccessful projects was the court's finding that BMQ substituted empirical trial-and-error for hypothesis-driven scientific investigation. Across the disallowed projects, Justice Lafleur identified four distinct methodological breakdowns that undermined BMQ's claim to have followed the scientific method. In four projects (B-10-05, B-10-07, B-11-01 and B-12-02), BMQ relied on a trial-and-error approach to reformulate mixes or find the causes of problems, and in one project (B-10-03) the court found that BMQ had not formulated any hypothesis at the start of the project. As the court emphasized, trial-and-error does not come within the scientific method if used alone.

Even more damaging to BMQ's evidentiary case was its response to experimental failure. In four separate instances among the disallowed projects, such as Project B-11-01 on chloride-ion permeability, when a tested concrete mixture produced an unwanted result or failed to meet the applicable standard, BMQ left that formulation aside or reformulated it without investigating why the failure occurred. Justice Lafleur repeatedly noted that BMQ did not seek to determine the causes of such results (for example, the drying rate of latex concrete in B-10-03, the increase in air content during hardening in B-10-08, the declining performance of the old superplasticizer in B-10-09, and the failure of certain mixes to meet the new standard in B-11-01), whereas, as Justice Bowman explained in Northwest Hydraulic, the rejection of a hypothesis after testing is itself an advance. The court characterized these activities as validating BMQ's mixes against industry standards and fine-tuning them rather than seeking to advance technological knowledge. Compounding these methodological flaws, BMQ failed across five disallowed projects to satisfy the court that it had followed the scientific method, presented oral testimony in four projects (B-10-03, B-10-08, B-10-12 and B-12-02) that was found unclear, implausible, or inconsistent with the documentary evidence or the technical narratives submitted on Form T661, and relied across all eight rejected projects on standard industry practices.
Failure to Demonstrate Scientific or Technological Advancement and Statutory Exclusions

The fourth Northwest Hydraulic criterion—reflecting paragraph (c) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Act—requires that the overall approach be undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement that increases the general technological knowledge base, rather than merely expanding the taxpayer's internal commercial product catalogue. As the Tax Court noted in Béton mobile du Québec, drawing on IC 86-4R3 and earlier decisions such as Flavor Net Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 179, and Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 21, there is a critical legal distinction between achieving a "technological advancement" and merely adapting a known technology or practice to a new situation where it is reasonably certain that the approach will work.

Justice Lafleur held that in the eight losing projects, BMQ failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that it sought to achieve any technological advancement. Instead, the court categorized BMQ's activities in those projects into three non-eligible classifications that trigger explicit statutory exclusions under subsection 248(1) of the Act. First, all eight losing projects were found to constitute standard practice and routine engineering: formulating concrete mixtures using newly released commercial cements, such as Ter-C3 in Projects B-10-05, B-10-07, and B-10-08, or commercial admixtures, such as the plasticizer in Project B-10-09, merely established internal operating recipes for BMQ's fleet without advancing concrete technology beyond what was already known in the field. Second, the court relied on the quality control or routine testing exclusion, which is statutorily excluded under paragraph 248(1)(f) of the Act. Specifically, Project B-10-09 (validating standard concretes with a new commercial plasticizer) was treated as routine testing, and Project B-11-01 was found to consist of controlling the compliance of existing products with a new standard by normal characterization tests, rather than resolving a fundamental scientific uncertainty. Third, the court found routine data collection, which is statutorily excluded under paragraph 248(1)(k) of the Act unless it is commensurate with and directly in support of core experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(d). In Projects B-10-03 (measuring the moisture content of a single 15% latex concrete mix at different ages using standard methods), B-10-09 and B-11-01 (study of chloride ion permeability and durability with various pozzolanic additions and cements, in which BMQ inventoried and tested its existing mixes and selected those that complied with the new standard without seeking to understand why others failed), the data collection was not done in support of SR&ED.
Contemporaneous Documentation Deficiencies and the Role of Oral Testimony

Perhaps the most instructive evidentiary analysis in Béton mobile du Québec concerns the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic: "Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?". Across all 14 projects—both the eight disallowed projects and the six allowed projects—BMQ failed to produce comprehensive, self-contained contemporaneous written records that explicitly documented the formulation of hypotheses, the detailed progression of each experimental iteration, and the causal analysis of test results as the work progressed.

This evidentiary deficiency created an acute litigation risk. However, Justice Lafleur's treatment of the fifth criterion demonstrates a vital nuance in Canadian tax litigation regarding the standard of proof: while contemporaneous documentation is the premier and most reliable form of evidence to establish SR&ED, the fifth Northwest Hydraulic question is an evidentiary indicator of whether a systematic investigation actually took place, rather than an absolute statutory bar that automatically invalidates a claim if written logs are incomplete.

For the six winning projects, Justice Lafleur found that, although no detailed contemporaneous record was kept, the documentation produced at the hearing together with the testimonial evidence—particularly that of Mr. Dubé for Projects B-10-18 and B-11-04 and that of Mr. Bertrand for Projects B-11-07, B-12-01, B-12-03 and B-12-07—demonstrated the progress of the activities. This evidence, together with the test results from independent laboratories, convinced the court on a balance of probabilities that BMQ had formulated hypotheses, followed the scientific method by adjusting its mixes in response to the results obtained, and sought or achieved technological advancement, even where, as in Project B-10-18, the desired product was not obtained. Conversely, for the eight losing projects, the decisive failures lay chiefly in the absence of technological uncertainty and advancement; in addition, in certain projects the witnesses' testimony was found unclear, implausible, or inconsistent with the documentary evidence or Form T661 (B-10-03, B-10-08, B-10-12 and B-12-02), and BMQ failed to discharge its evidentiary burden.
Commercial Contract Pre-Qualification, Subcontractor Fees, and Materials Vetting

The decision also illuminates the contractual and expenditure-vetting pitfalls confronting manufacturers who develop custom formulations in response to customer tenders or infrastructure specifications. As noted in the court's review of BMQ's operational context, usually before a contract was awarded to BMQ—particularly a public-sector contract—the concrete mix to be supplied was pre-approved by the client and the contractor, since the concrete had to comply with minimum industry standards.

Where the mixes tested had already been pre-approved and were placed commercially on clients' worksites on the same day as sampling or before laboratory results were known, as occurred in Projects B-10-05, B-10-07 and B-10-08, the court treated this as evidence that no real technological uncertainty existed, and in Project B-10-08 it characterized the large-scale trials as commercial activities whose costs should not be included in the SR&ED claim. Moreover, following the sequential two-stage rule applied by Justice Lafleur, because Projects B-10-03, B-10-05, B-10-07, B-10-08, B-10-09, B-10-12, B-11-01, and B-12-02 failed at the project-eligibility threshold, none of their associated salaries, subcontractor testing invoices and raw material costs were allowed, although the court nonetheless indicated for each project the amounts that would have been deductible had the activities qualified. Only for the six eligible projects were the specific expenditures allowed for reassessment, after adjustments that included removing hours not directly related to SR&ED and reducing salary claims by 10% because Mr. Dubé admitted to rounding the hours on the time sheets.

Where a project passes the first-stage eligibility threshold, raw materials used in experimental batches or trial production runs qualify under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 127(9) of the Act and CRA policy on manufacturing SR&ED only if they are "materials consumed"—meaning the material was destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED—or "materials transformed," meaning material that has been changed or incorporated into another material or product as a result of the SR&ED and retains some value to the claimant or another party. To claim materials used in trial production runs on commercial equipment such as BMQ's mobile concrete mixers, a claimant must determine that the production run was strictly required for SR&ED, identify the specific section of the commercial facility or equipment and personnel involved, establish the exact duration of each production run required to evaluate or validate the SR&ED, and account for any commercial value retained by the output.
3. Comparative Summary Table: Statutory Criteria, Taxpayer Failures, and Judicial Standard of Proof

The following table synthesizes the legal and technical requirements examined by Justice Lafleur in Béton mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 278), contrasting the specific evidentiary and methodological failures in BMQ's eight disallowed projects with the findings in the six allowed projects and the governing standard of proof in the Tax Court of Canada.

Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Disallowed Projects (8 Projects)
Contrasting Success Factors in Allowed Projects (6 Projects)
Court's Evidentiary Standard of Proof & Adjudicative Rule

cells: 1. Scientific or Technological Uncertainty
Subsection 248(1) of the Act; Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 1; IC 86-4R3.

Conflated internal unfamiliarity with new commercial inputs (Ter-C3 ternary cement, commercial plasticizers, pozzolans) with true technological uncertainty; limitations were resolvable via existing industry knowledge and standard mix-design practices (failed in all 8 losing projects).

Demonstrated uncertainty that standard procedures could not remove, arising from the mobile mixer's shorter, less forceful mixing, the untested combination of known components (e.g., 20% air content in B-10-18; fast-setting self-compacting concrete in B-11-04), underwater placement (B-11-07), latex-free quick-setting concrete (B-12-01), use of latex concrete as a bridge running surface (B-12-03) and new roller-compacted concrete repair products (B-12-07).

Balance of probabilities resting on the taxpayer. Must prove an objective knowledge gap in the field of science or technology that a competent professional cannot resolve using publicly available knowledge or routine engineering.
2. Formulation of Causal Hypotheses
Subsection 248(1) of the Act; Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 2 (Stage (d) of Justice Bowman's 5-stage process).

Failed to articulate testable causal hypotheses explaining why chemical or physical interactions occurred; relied on trial-and-error in 4 projects, had no hypothesis in 1 project (B-10-03), and in 4 instances did not investigate the cause of an unwanted result.

Formulated hypotheses that the court accepted, for example that adding a foaming admixture, an air-entraining admixture and air injection would increase air content (B-10-18), that modifying the superplasticizer would improve air content (B-11-07), and that certain superplasticizers could give concrete the properties provided by latex (B-12-01).

Balance of probabilities. Requires proof of a hypothesis, i.e., a statement to be tested by an experiment or trial, specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the identified technological uncertainty.
3. Systematic Investigation or Search (Scientific Method)
Preamble of subsection 248(1) of the Act; Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 3 (Stages (a)–(e) of Bowman's process).

Failed to prove adherence to the scientific method in 5 projects; relied on standard industry testing procedures in 8 instances; witness testimony was unclear or contradicted the documentary evidence or Form T661 narratives in 4 instances.
Tests performed scientifically, largely by independent laboratories, with mix dosages modified in response to the results obtained and, in B-12-07, mixes compared under similar conditions.

Balance of probabilities. Must demonstrate adoption of the entire scientific method—observation, objective, hypothesis, controlled experimentation/analysis, and logical conclusion—distinguishing the work from ad hoc trial-and-error.
4. Scientific or Technological Advancement & Statutory Exclusions
Paragraphs 248(1)(a)–(c) and Exclusions 248(1)(f) & (k) of the Act; Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 4.

Work sought only to validate or fine-tune existing mixes against standards; classified by the Court as ineligible "standard practice" (8 projects), excluded "quality control / routine testing" (B-10-09; compliance testing in B-11-01), or excluded "routine data collection" (B-10-03, B-10-09, B-11-01).

Work generated new knowledge, such as the energy limits and short mixing time of the mobile mixer (B-10-18), a fast-setting feature incorporated into self-compacting concrete (B-11-04), the effect of new superplasticizers on compressive strength and latex replacement (B-11-07, B-12-01), and new methods for repairing roller-compacted concrete (B-12-07).

Balance of probabilities. The inquiry focuses on whether the work sought to advance the general scientific or technological knowledge base (even if the experiment ultimately failed), rather than achieving routine incremental product adaptations.
5. Contemporaneous Record of Hypotheses and Results
Subsection 248(1) and section 230 of the Act; Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 5.

Failed across all projects to produce comprehensive contemporaneous logs explicitly mapping hypotheses to progressive test results; in four losing projects (B-10-03, B-10-08, B-10-12, B-12-02), the testimony was also found unclear, implausible, or inconsistent with the documentary evidence or Form T661.

Despite the absence of a detailed contemporaneous record, the documentation produced at the hearing and the testimonial evidence—particularly that of Mr. Dubé (B-10-18, B-11-04) and Mr. Bertrand (B-11-07, B-12-01, B-12-03, B-12-07)—demonstrated the progress of the activities.

Evidentiary indicator weighed on a balance of probabilities. Contemporaneous documentation is strongly preferred; while credible oral testimony can legally bridge documentary gaps at trial, unclear testimony combined with poor records is fatal.
6. Two-Stage Expenditure Vetting (Subcontractors & Materials)
Paragraphs 248(1)(d) & (i), Section 37, and Subsection 127(9) of the Act; Zeuter Development / Béton mobile rule.

Because the 8 projects failed the Step 1 project-level eligibility test, none of the associated labour, material, and third-party subcontractor testing expenditures were allowed, although the Court indicated for each the amounts that would have been deductible had the work qualified.

Satisfied Step 1 project eligibility, permitting the reassessment and allowance of directly supporting engineering labour, materials consumed/transformed in experimental batches, and eligible subcontractor testing fees.

Sequential two-stage legal test. Step 1: Project must satisfy all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria. Step 2: Only if Step 1 is met are specific expenditures vetted to confirm they were directly in support of and commensurate with the SR&ED needs.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the holdings of Béton mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 278) into actionable legal and technical compliance protocols for Canadian taxpayers, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic industrial R&D initiatives that mirror the exact pitfalls identified by Justice Lafleur. Each case study outlines the initial vulnerability profile and demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contractual terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the court's objections and satisfy subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act.
Case Study 1: Specialty Cementitious Materials and Precast/Mobile Infrastructure Manufacturing
Fact Pattern and Initial Vulnerability Profile

St-Laurent Infrastructure Concrete Ltd. ("SLIC"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) operating in Quebec and Ontario, manufactures ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) and mobile-mixed rapid-repair mortars for municipal bridge decks and hydroelectric spillways. SLIC undertakes a project titled "Development of a Low-Carbon Ternary-Blended Rapid-Set Mortar for Sub-Zero Bridge Deck Overlays." A provincial transportation ministry issues a tender requiring a bridge overlay mortar that achieves a compressive strength of 20 MPa within 3 hours at ambient temperatures of −5 °C, a rapid chloride permeability below 1,000 coulombs at 28 days (ASTM C1202), and a 40% reduction in Portland cement clinker using supplementary cementitious materials consisting of calcined clay and limestone filler. SLIC mixes the mortar on-site using truck-mounted continuous volumetric auger mixers.

In its initial posture, SLIC exhibits four acute compliance deficiencies that directly mirror BMQ's eight disallowed projects. First, echoing Projects B-10-05, B-10-07, B-10-09, and B-11-01, SLIC's engineers describe the project in internal memoranda as "characterizing a new commercial calcined clay binder and polycarboxylate superplasticizer to pre-qualify for the Ministry bridge tender". Second, echoing Project B-11-01, SLIC's laboratory technician runs 18 batch mixes varying the percentages of calcined clay, calcium sulfoaluminate (CSA) accelerator, and citric acid retarder; when Batches 4 through 9 flash-set inside the auger mixer within 45 seconds or fail the 3-hour 20 MPa compression test, the technician simply marks "FAIL – Discarded" on the batch sheet and switches to a different chemical supplier without analyzing why the flash-set occurred. Third, SLIC's batch sheets record only the weights of raw materials, slump flow, and 3-hour and 28-day compressive strengths—identical to routine quality control sheets excluded under paragraph 248(1)(f) of the Act. Fourth, SLIC claims $140,000 in raw materials poured during a commercial bridge repair contract and $45,000 in fees paid to an external materials testing laboratory for standard ASTM C1202 chloride-permeability certification reports required by the Ministry contract. Under Justice Lafleur's analytical framework in Béton mobile du Québec, a CRA Research and Technology Advisor and the Tax Court of Canada would disallow SLIC's entire claim at Step 1 for failing to distinguish the work from standard mix-design practice, relying on trial-and-error, abandoning failed mixes without causal investigation, and performing routine data collection and quality assurance.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance and Establishing the Baseline of Technological Uncertainty

To satisfy the first Northwest Hydraulic criterion, SLIC must restructure its project governance prior to commencing experimental work by instituting a formal Gate-Zero Technological Baseline Protocol. Rather than stating vaguely at audit or trial that "literature was consulted," SLIC's lead engineer must compile a dated Gate-Zero Technical Dossier archiving specific peer-reviewed papers, CSA A23.1 standards, and chemical admixture technical data sheets. This dossier must objectively demonstrate why publicly available knowledge and standard industry practice are insufficient: while ternary calcined-clay blends and CSA rapid-set cements are individually known, existing chemical hydration models show that introducing high dosages of calcium sulfoaluminate alongside calcined clay in a high-shear, 12-second residence-time volumetric auger mixer at −5 °C induces competitive sulfate-aluminate depletion and unpredicted ettringite precipitation kinetics.

In doing so, SLIC's governance charter must decouple the commercial product objective—meeting the Ministry's 20 MPa in 3 hours and 1,000-coulomb tender specification—from the underlying technological uncertainty. The technological uncertainty is formally defined in the project charter as whether and how the antagonistic ionic interaction between calcined clay metakaolin aluminates, lithium-carbonate accelerators, and polycarboxylate ether side-chains can be stabilized during ultra-short (10-to-15-second) low-temperature mechanical hydration to prevent premature false-setting while sustaining exothermic silicate and ettringite nucleation at −5 °C. Simultaneously, any preliminary baseline testing conducted to verify the moisture content, fineness, or standard dosage curve of a supplier's calcined clay or plasticizer—analogous to BMQ's disallowed Projects B-10-03, B-10-07, and B-10-09—is ring-fenced into a separate, non-claimed internal cost centre so that routine material characterization does not contaminate the core experimental development claim.
Step 2: Experimentation Tracking and Eliminating the "Trial-and-Error" Pitfall

To overcome Justice Lafleur's condemnation of trial-and-error and the abandonment of failed tests, SLIC must replace standard batch sheets with a mandatory Iterative Hypothesis-Experiment-Analysis (H-E-A) Protocol. Under this protocol, no experimental batch may be mixed without a signed pre-test causal hypothesis statement predicting the physical and chemical mechanism under investigation. For example, prior to running Series 2, the lead engineer formulates Hypothesis H-2.1, postulating that if the side-chain density of the polycarboxylate superplasticizer is increased from a 1:2 to a 1:4 carboxylate-to-ester ratio while buffering the mixing water with 0.15% sodium gluconate, steric hindrance will delay aluminate adsorption onto calcined clay platelets during the initial 12-second auger shear phase, thereby extending working time from 45 seconds to over 18 minutes without suppressing 3-hour ettringite crystallization at −5 °C.

Directly addressing the fatal flaw identified by Justice Lafleur in four of BMQ's disallowed project instances, SLIC's engineering governance strictly prohibits discarding a failed batch without conducting a documented post-mortem diagnostic analysis. When Batch 6 flash-sets or fails compressive strength, SLIC performs isothermal calorimetry, pore-solution ion chromatography, and ultrasonic pulse velocity tracking to determine why the hypothesis failed—discovering, for instance, that the calcined clay's high specific surface area adsorbed 65% of the sodium gluconate retarder within the first 4 seconds of auger mixing, starving the liquid phase. That analytical conclusion is then formally recorded and used to formulate Hypothesis H-2.2, which tests pre-saturating the supplementary binder or modifying the sequence of admixture injection in the mobile mixer manifold.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation Architecture

To cure the fifth Northwest Hydraulic deficiency that plagued all 14 of BMQ's projects and ensure that SLIC does not have to rely solely on the memory and viva voce testimony of its engineers nine years later in the Tax Court of Canada, SLIC implements a Contemporaneous SR&ED Evidence Repository using version-controlled Electronic Laboratory Notebooks (ELNs). Every experimental iteration is logged in real time with immutable timestamps recording the Hypothesis ID, the controlled independent variables versus constant baseline parameters, the quantitative raw sensor and laboratory data (including calorimetry curves, rheology yield-stress measurements, and auger torque logs), and the scientific conclusion linking the results to the next iteration. Prior to filing Form T661, SLIC's R&D tax counsel and lead engineer audit the technical narrative against the ELN records to ensure complete concordance between the contemporaneous logs and the T661 text, eliminating the evidentiary credibility gap noted by Justice Lafleur in four of BMQ's disallowed projects.
Step 4: Contractual Structuring and Expenditure Vetting

To protect the eligibility of subcontractor fees and materials under sections 37 and 127 of the Act, SLIC restructures both its commercial and testing agreements. Standard ASTM C1202 certification tests on the final commercial mix required for Ministry tender pre-qualification are recognized as excluded quality control or routine testing under paragraph 248(1)(f) and removed from the claim. Conversely, statements of work (SOWs) issued to third-party university or commercial laboratories during the experimental phase explicitly specify that the subcontractor is performing non-routine analytical testing—such as scanning electron microscopy or X-ray diffraction of failed hydration matrices—directly in support of SLIC's experimental hypotheses under paragraph 248(1)(d), with SLIC retaining all intellectual property and bearing the full financial risk. Finally, when SLIC transitions from laboratory batches to full-scale mobile mixer trials, SLIC executes a formal Experimental Production Run Authorization specifying the exact duration, equipment, and personnel required to validate the SR&ED. Test slabs poured at SLIC's test yard that are cored, subjected to destructive freeze-thaw testing, and subsequently crushed and disposed of are documented with disposal receipts as "materials consumed" (rendered virtually valueless), whereas any trial batch poured on a client's commercial site that remains in service is excluded from "materials consumed" and accounted for strictly under the commercial production and "materials transformed" rules.
Case Study 2: Advanced Industrial Process Engineering and Automated Chemical Mixing Systems
Fact Pattern and Initial Vulnerability Profile

Boréal Polymer Composites Inc. ("BPCI"), a Canadian industrial manufacturer, designs and operates continuous mobile and in-plant reactive extrusion and mixing systems used to manufacture rapid-curing elastomeric sealants and structural adhesives for civil infrastructure. BPCI claims SR&ED for a project titled "Optimization of a Latex-Free Reactive Polyurethane-Silane Screed and Continuous High-Shear Mixing Head," which combines elements analogous to BMQ's disallowed Project B-12-02 on improving quick-setting concrete and Project B-10-03 on moisture determination, alongside BMQ's allowed Project B-12-01 and B-12-03 concepts. BPCI sought to eliminate toxic isocyanate and styrene-butadiene latex modifiers from its structural screed while upgrading its mobile mixing head to dispense the new high-viscosity formulation at 5 °C without air entrapment or moisture-induced foaming.

In its initial posture, BPCI faces four critical litigation vulnerabilities identified in Béton mobile du Québec. First, echoing Project B-12-02, BPCI's Form T661 narrative describes the project as "improving our existing quick-setting screed product and adjusting pump pressures and nozzle geometries on our mixing head to improve flow rates," inviting immediate classification as routine engineering or standard practice. Second, whenever moisture in the mineral fillers caused micro-foaming in the extruded screed, shop-floor operators adjusted auger RPM, vacuum degassing pressure, or moisture-scavenger additive levels empirically on the fly; once a visually smooth screed was achieved, testing ceased immediately without investigating the thermodynamic or fluid-dynamic relationship between shear heating, filler moisture desorption, and silane crosslinking. Third, BPCI claimed 100% of the salaries of four mechanical engineers and six shop technicians over 14 months based on year-end management estimates, without contemporaneous time-tracking linking their activities to specific experimental hypotheses under paragraph 248(1)(d). Fourth, BPCI entered into a supply agreement with a major general contractor that included a $200,000 milestone payment for "customizing and testing the latex-free screed for the Metro Tunnel Project," raising the rules on contract payments under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the Act.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance to Isolate Core Experimental Development from Support Engineering

To survive the Tax Court's strict distinction between ineligible "routine engineering" and eligible "experimental development" supported by commensurate engineering under paragraphs 248(1)(c) and (d) of the Act, BPCI restructures its project architecture into a Dual-Tier SR&ED Governance Model. BPCI's Technical Steering Committee formally charters the project around the coupled chemo-mechanical system uncertainty: existing rheological and fluid-dynamics models cannot predict the non-Newtonian shear-thickening transition and moisture-vapor cavitation threshold of a silane-terminated polyurethane paste loaded with 65% graded quartz aggregate when subjected to shear rates exceeding 500 s⁻¹ inside a continuous twin-auger mixing chamber. Achieving rapid cure in under 20 minutes without latex polymers while suppressing shear-induced exothermic temperature spikes above 60 °C—which trigger premature moisture outgassing from the aggregate micropores and structural micro-foaming—requires advancing technological knowledge of coupled high-shear heat transfer and silane hydrolysis kinetics. Under this governance charter, mechanical CAD design of modified auger flights, finite element analysis, and sensor instrumentation are explicitly documented not as standalone equipment updates, which would be disallowed as routine engineering, but as paragraph 248(1)(d) support activities strictly commensurate with and directly in support of constructing the experimental apparatus needed to test the core thermo-rheological hypotheses.
Step 2: Implementing a Rigorous Design of Experiments (DoE) Protocol

To prevent the Tax Court from characterizing shop-floor adjustments as "trial-and-error" as Justice Lafleur did in BMQ's disallowed projects, BPCI mandates a structured Design of Experiments (DoE) and Causal Diagnostic Protocol. Instead of ad hoc operator adjustments, BPCI's engineers establish a formal multi-variable DoE matrix isolating four independent parameters: auger pitch-to-diameter ratio (0.5, 0.75, and 1.0), organofunctional alkoxysilane molecular weight distribution, zeolite molecular-sieve moisture scavenger pore size (3 Å versus 4 Å), and specific mechanical energy input (0.05–0.15 kWh/kg). When Trial Run #7 exhibits micro-foaming and a 35% drop in flexural modulus, testing does not stop or pivot blindly. Instead, engineers extract core samples, perform micro-CT porosity mapping and Karl Fischer titration of free versus bound water, and plot inline infrared thermography data against auger shear stress. The resulting analytical report demonstrates that local shear heating at the auger tip exceeded 75 °C, causing bound crystal water in the filler to desorb faster than the 3 Å zeolite kinetics could capture—directly generating the revised hypothesis for Trial Run #8, which tests introducing a reverse-flight decompression zone in the auger geometry to cap peak shear temperature at 55 °C.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Documentation and Granular Time-Tracking

To ensure that BPCI satisfies the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion through self-sustaining documentary evidence rather than gambling on oral testimony at trial years later, BPCI deploys an integrated Contemporaneous SR&ED Audit Trail. At the close of every two-week sprint, the lead R&D engineer signs a dated SR&ED Hypothesis and Results Ledger that links each DoE run number to the specific hypothesis tested, the raw telemetry files, the analytical conclusion, and the resulting advancement in technological knowledge. Simultaneously, rather than relying on retrospective year-end estimates, all engineers and technicians log hours daily against specific SR&ED Project and Hypothesis Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) codes that segregate experimental testing and direct support machining from non-SR&ED commercial activities such as routine equipment maintenance, operator training, or standard quality control.
Step 4: Restructuring Customer Contracts to Avoid "Contract Payment" Disqualification

To neutralize the risk that the general contractor's $200,000 payment is classified as a disqualifying "contract payment" as defined in subsection 127(9) of the Act—which, under subsection 127(18), reduces the qualified expenditures in a claimant's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool where a third party contracts for the performance of SR&ED on its behalf—BPCI's tax counsel restructures the commercial agreement prior to execution. The agreement with the general contractor is drafted strictly as a standard commercial product supply contract for the delivery of finished structural screed meeting commercial performance warranty thresholds at a fixed unit price per metric ton, with no contractual obligation for BPCI to perform R&D services, no deliverable of test data or research reports to the contractor, and explicit contractual retention of all background and foreground intellectual property, patents, and formulation trade secrets by BPCI. Any field trials conducted at the contractor's site to validate the experimental auger head under real-world tunnel humidity conditions are governed by a separate Site Access and Experimental Testing Addendum under which BPCI bears 100% of the cost of scraping, removing, and replacing any experimental screed section that fails performance metrics, proving that BPCI bore the full technical and financial risk of the experimental development.
5. Summary of Remedial Governance Controls Versus Disqualification Triggers in 2019 TCC 278

The table below consolidates the operational, documentary, and contractual transformations demonstrated in the two remedial case studies against the exact judicial failure points identified by Justice Lafleur in Béton mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen.

headers: Disqualification Trigger in Béton mobile du Québec (2019 TCC 278)

cells: Problem Definition & Baseline Knowledge
Relying on unverified assertions that existing literature did not cover mobile mixers; testing known commercial inputs (Ter-C3 cement, plasticizers) via standard mix design.

Gate-Zero Technological Baseline Dossier: Archiving dated literature, standards, and chemical/mechanical calculations proving why system-level interactions cannot be predicted by competent professionals.
Establishes Scientific or Technological Uncertainty (Criterion 1) on a balance of probabilities and refutes CRA allegations of "routine engineering".
Experimental Methodology & Failure Handling
Adjusting mix proportions by empirical trial-and-error; stopping testing immediately upon encountering an unwanted commercial result without investigating the cause of failure.

Iterative H-E-A & Root-Cause Failure Protocol: Requiring a written causal hypothesis before every test and mandating quantitative diagnostic analysis (calorimetry, microscopy, telemetry) of every failed batch to drive the next hypothesis.
Satisfies Hypothesis Formulation (Criterion 2) and Systematic Investigation (Criterion 3), proving adherence to Justice Bowman's 5-stage scientific method.
Scope of Claimed Activities & Exclusions
Claiming standalone material characterization (B-10-07, B-10-09), moisture verification (B-10-03), and permeability data compilation (B-11-01).

WBS Ring-Fencing & Dual-Tier Chartering: Excluding routine material characterization, QA/QC, and commercial pre-qualification from the SR&ED claim; linking all paragraph 248(1)(d) engineering and testing directly to core paragraph 248(1)(c) hypotheses.
Demonstrates genuine Technological Advancement (Criterion 4) and immunizes the claim against statutory exclusions under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k) of the Act.
Contemporaneous Documentation & Trial Readiness

Failing across all 14 projects to keep contemporaneous logs mapping progressive hypotheses to test results; relying on witness memory 9 years later, with unclear, implausible or contradictory testimony on 4 losing projects.

Contemporaneous ELN & T661 Concordance Audit: Real-time Electronic Lab Notebooks logging Hypothesis → Variable Matrix → Raw Data → Causal Conclusion, cross-audited against Form T661 narratives prior to filing.
Satisfies Contemporaneous Record-Keeping (Criterion 5) directly via documentary proof, eliminating reliance on viva voce rescue at trial and facilitating early administrative resolution with the CRA.
Contractual Terms & Expenditure Segregation
Conducting mix validation to pre-qualify for customer contracts; losing 100% of subcontractor and material expenditures on the 8 disqualified projects under the two-stage inquiry rule.

Commercial Supply Bifurcation & Trial Run Authorizations: Drafting customer contracts strictly for finished goods (retaining IP and financial risk); issuing paragraph 248(1)(d) analytical SOWs to subcontractors; documenting destruction of consumed trial materials.
Satisfies Step 1 project eligibility and Step 2 expenditure vetting under sections 37 and 127 of the Act, preserving full ITC recovery for internal labour, subcontractors, and consumed materials.

body.text: 6. Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Béton mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 278) stands as a critical precedent for manufacturing, materials engineering, and industrial process claimants across Canada. While the ruling confirms that innovations in traditional industrial sectors—such as concrete formulation and mobile mixing technology—can successfully qualify for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits when genuine system-level chemical and physical uncertainties are resolved through the scientific method, as demonstrated by BMQ's six allowed projects, the dismissal of BMQ's remaining eight projects underscores the unforgiving nature of the five cumulative criteria in Northwest Hydraulic.

Three overarching legal imperatives emerge from Justice Lafleur's decision for Canadian tax advisors and R&D directors. First, technological uncertainty cannot be inferred merely because a company is adapting newly commercialized raw materials, such as ternary cements or advanced admixtures, to specialized equipment or harsh climatic conditions; the taxpayer must objectively prove why existing scientific principles and standard industry mix-design procedures cannot predict the system's behaviour. Second, the hallmark of an eligible systematic investigation is how the taxpayer responds to experimental failure: abandoning an unsuccessful formulation to try another recipe is fatal evidence of routine trial-and-error, whereas conducting diagnostic analysis to determine why a formulation failed and using that knowledge to formulate a subsequent causal hypothesis is the essence of the scientific method. Finally, although the documentation produced at the hearing, combined with credible testimony from BMQ's engineers—particularly Mr. Bertrand and Mr. Dubé—allowed the court to find that the scientific method was followed in the six allowed projects despite the absence of detailed contemporaneous records, relying on oral testimony to cure deficient contemporaneous documentation is an expensive and high-risk litigation strategy. Integrating hypothesis-driven experimental logs, strict statutory exclusion screening, and disciplined contractual structuring directly into day-to-day engineering workflows remains the only reliable defence against CRA audit reassessments.
